title: Why Silicon Valley can’t slow down AI on its own

### Everyone says AI is moving too fast [[00:00:00]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=0)

**Luisa Rodriguez:** I’ve been getting really freaked out by how quickly things are moving in AI. And it turns out I’m not alone: [two thirds of Americans](https://www.pewresearch.org/chart/roughly-two-thirds-of-americans-say-ai-is-advancing-too-quickly/), [across the political spectrum](https://apnorc.org/projects/most-adults-think-ai-is-developing-too-fast/), think AI is moving too fast.

And it’s not just the public. The people who are building AI, the people who are literally setting the pace, [agree](https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/).

And it’s about to get even faster. AI is now helping build the next generation of AI. One of Anthropic’s cofounders thinks it could be [improving itself with no humans involved](https://importai.substack.com/p/import-ai-476-creativity-and-rsi) as soon as next year — so, 2027.

Politicians are getting freaked out too, and that includes [people on both sides of the aisle](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/15/nx-s1-5968678/bernie-sanders-and-steve-bannon-and-ai), which I find especially wild.

The public wants to slow down. The people building AI want to slow down. Lots of politicians want to slow down. So why the hell aren’t we slowing down?

You might feel like you personally don’t need to understand this issue. But I seriously believe this is a conversation everyone should be a part of, not just CEOs and a handful of policymakers.

The rules we end up with will be shaped by what voters understand and ask for. So it matters that people like you and me actually understand the options.

Let’s dig in.

### What exactly would we be slowing down? [[00:01:28]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=88)

First things first. When people hear “slow down AI,” a lot of them picture someone pulling the plug on ChatGPT.

We could actually stop them building anything more powerful tomorrow, and you could still use ChatGPT or Claude or Gemini exactly like you do today. Businesses could keep finding new uses for them. Researchers could keep studying them.

And honestly, we’re nowhere near making the most of the AI that we already have. Today’s models alone could still transform science, medicine, and the economy. We’ve barely scratched the surface.

So the real question is how to slow down the race to build AI that is _even more powerful_ than what we have now.

### Let the companies race ahead [[00:02:13]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=133)

Let’s start with what we’re doing now: basically letting the companies race ahead, and trusting them to hit the brakes if things get dangerous.

The CEOs supposedly want to do this, so why not just let them?

And to be fair, every so often, one of them does tap the brakes. A couple of months ago, OpenAI found that its new model, Astra, was [extremely good at hacking](https://openai.com/index/responding-next-frontier-critical-cyber-capabilities/). So it did something AI companies almost never do: it [paused its biggest training run](https://openai.com/index/pacing-model-development-cyber-capabilities/) for a few weeks to tighten its security and run more safety tests.

That was an expensive decision, which is admirable, but it’s not the end of the story.

The researchers running the safety tests found that around half the time, Astra [could tell it was being tested](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra). Maybe that doesn’t sound like a big deal, but it is. If an AI knows it’s being tested, then when it behaves well, you can’t tell whether it’s actually safe or just on its best behaviour.

And there was another issue. One of the best ways we have for knowing what an AI is up to is reading a written log of its reasoning, called the [chain of thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473). When Astra was told someone was reading its chain of thought, it suddenly started writing down a lot less of it. So the two main ways we check whether an AI is safe — watching how it behaves in tests and reading its reasoning — have both started to break down.

The testers told OpenAI they couldn’t tell whether Astra was safe, and OpenAI [released it anyway](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/).

Every week a company holds back, its rivals can release a better model, winning over more customers, more investors, and the best researchers.So even if every one of them agrees a slowdown would make AI safer, none of them wants to slow down first.

They’ve even written this into their own rules. In 2025, OpenAI [updated its safety framework](https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/) to say it might relax its own safety requirements if a competitor released a high-risk system without them. Their own rules say: “If someone else cuts corners, we might have to as well.”

And that competitive pressure is about to get much, much worse. Because AI is increasingly doing the work of building the next generations of AI. OpenAI says its agents now put in [about three days of work](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) for every one day worked by its human researchers.

Here’s why that makes slowing down so much harder. Let’s say OpenAI pauses for a month. Today, that would mean all of its competitors get about a month ahead.

Now imagine a competitor like Anthropic gets to the point where its AI can do [literally all of the work of AI research](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement): not just writing code, but also deciding what to try, figuring out what worked, and choosing what’s next. That AI doesn’t need to sleep or take weekends off. And it isn’t just one researcher. Anthropic could run thousands of copies at once, all working in parallel around the clock.

So while OpenAI is paused, Anthropic’s not just doing a month’s worth of research. Their army of AI researchers could be doing several months’ worth, and getting better at it the whole time. So the gap doesn’t just stay the same: it grows.

We don’t actually know what happens if AIs take over all of AI research, but [many experts believe](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/toby-ord-recursive-self-improvement-agi-timelines/) this is how things would play out.

And that’s exactly why I don’t think we can just trust the companies to slow down on their own. Someone needs to set rules that apply to all of them at once.

### Require companies to pass safety checkpoints [[00:06:03]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=363)

So what would these rules look like?

One of the least heavy-handed versions would let companies keep building more and more powerful AI until a model reaches a certain level of dangerous capability.

Think of it a bit like building a skyscraper. You wouldn’t tell a construction company that it has to build at half its normal speed. You’d tell them: before you add more floors, prove the building’s safe. And if the engineers find a crack in the foundations, you stop building upwards until it’s fixed.

For AI, those checkpoints would be triggered by dangerous capabilities.

Maybe it’s become extremely good at hacking. Or maybe it can [work competently on its own](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/beth-barnes-ai-safety-evals/) for very long stretches. At that point, the company would have to prove it could keep the model under control. And if it couldn’t prove that, it would have to stop making the model more powerful until it could.

There’s a lot I like about this idea, but it raises two really hard questions.

First, what counts as a dangerous capability? If a model can help someone break into a single company’s network, does that raise the alarm? What if it can take down a power grid on its own? Or what if it can help someone design a biological weapon? We’d have to decide where to draw those lines.

The companies do have rough versions already. For example, Anthropic sorts its models into [AI safety levels](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy), modelled on the [biosafety levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosafety_level) that decide which biology labs get to work with everything from flu to Ebola.

Some of these lines are actually pretty clear already. Can it find security flaws nobody knew about in software billions of people use? That’s a yes-or-no question, and Astra [answered yes](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra).

But a bunch of them aren’t totally clear. And the problem is that each company draws its own lines, grades its own models, and can redraw them whenever it likes.

Under a real checkpoint system, someone independent, like an auditor or government body, would figure out where the lines are and enforce them.

But that leads to a second and, in my opinion, much harder question: how would we even know a model was safe? What evidence would actually be convincing?

Researchers have caught AI models [deliberately doing badly on tests](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/research/scheming-reasoning-evaluations) when they work out that doing too well will mean they’re not deployed. They’ve also caught models [pretending to go along with their training](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking) while privately planning to do something else in the future.

When Astra came out, OpenAI called it “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.” But that was all based on tests that Astra could often tell were tests. So when OpenAI assures me that Astra is safe because it passed their safety tests, I am not convinced.

And that’s frustrating, because I really like the logic of checkpoints. The slowdown lasts exactly as long as it needs to. If a company can show it’s safe straight away, there’s barely any delay. If a problem takes six months or several years to fix, it waits that long. But checkpoints are only as good as our safety tests. And right now, our safety tests aren’t good enough.

Checkpoints have another problem. They usually kick in once a model is already close to dangerous. And by then, the model already exists. It could be [stolen by hackers](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sella-nevo-securing-ai-model-weights/), or, if it’s capable enough, try to escape on its own. That’s why some experts think checkpoints come too late. They want to slow things down before we get anywhere near AI models that are plausibly very dangerous.

### Put a speed limit on AI development [[00:09:38]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=578)

A speed limit works differently. Instead of waiting for something dangerous to show up, you limit how fast companies can go in the first place.

The most obvious way to do that is to limit computing power. Building a cutting-edge AI model takes an absolutely enormous number of specialised computer chips, all running together in [giant data centres](https://epoch.ai/topics/data-centers).

More computing power has been [one of the main ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_scaling_law) companies have made their AI smarter so far, so governments could set a ceiling. No company gets to use more than a certain amount of computing power to train a single model, and that ceiling only goes up slowly over time.

But there are problems with this approach too. One is that computing power isn’t the same thing as intelligence. It’s a bit like limiting how much fuel a car can use. That works until engineers figure out how to build a more efficient engine. Then the car goes faster on the same tank.

And that’s exactly what AI researchers do all the time. In early 2025, a Chinese company called DeepSeek [released a model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) that rivalled the best American ones, despite reportedly being trained using a fraction of the computing power.

Still, I think this is one of the better tools we’ve got. Computing power is one of the few things in AI that we can [actually measure and track](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/lennart-heim-compute-governance/): where the chips are, how many there are, and what they’re being used for.

To me, the biggest problem with compute limits is that they wouldn’t stop AI from doing more and more of the work building the next generation of AI models.

### Limit how much AI can help build AI [[00:11:11]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=671)

So another version of slowing down would specifically limit how much AI companies can use internal AI systems to automate their own AI research.

The idea isn’t to keep AI companies from ever using their AI models as they work. Companies could still use it for ordinary coding and science. What you’d restrict is the kind of automated AI research that could send AI progress into overdrive.

The hard part is figuring out where helping ends and AI building AI begins. An AI that fixes a typo in some training code is helping AI research. But so is a whole fleet of AIs that plan and run thousands of experiments.

In 2025, Google DeepMind’s [AlphaEvolve](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/) found a way to speed up a key step in training its Gemini models by 23%, cutting total training time by about 1%. Is that ordinary help, or AI improving AI? Honestly, it’s hard to say.

But as [Ezra Klein has argued](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/20/opinion/ai-ban-self-improvement-recursive-models.html), we don’t need to find exactly where the perfect line would be. We just need a clear one.

A couple of years ago, AI companies weren’t handing their code over to AI. Now, at some companies, [most of it is written by AI](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement). So as a first step, Klein says, we could just go back to a world where none of the code is written by AI.

That’s pretty blunt, and it would slow things down a lot. Some people, like the economist Tyler Cowen, [think it wouldn’t work](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/banning-self-recursive-improvement-in-ai-models.html). But even the CEO of Anthropic has written that AI improving itself could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.

If that’s true, in my opinion, a clear, blunt line is a lot better than no line at all.

### Pause the development of more powerful AI altogether [[00:13:04]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=784)

OK, here’s the last idea, and it’s definitely the most drastic one. Some researchers think none of this goes far enough.

We don’t know how to reliably control AI that’s much more capable than what we have today. And there’s no guarantee that slowing down for a year or two would give us enough time to figure that out. So rather than building more powerful AI more slowly, they want to stop building it altogether, at least until we’re much more confident it’s safe.

David Krueger, who helped set up the UK’s AI Security Institute, has called for an [immediate, indefinite international ban](https://www.ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/state-of-emergency-montreal-based-ai-expert-says-industry-slowdown-plan-doesnt-go-far-enough/) on building more powerful AI.

And Bernie Sanders has [introduced a bill](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/9/23/us-lawmakers-propose-sweeping-ai-restrictions-with-superintelligence-ban) that would temporarily pause advanced AI development and permanently ban superintelligence.

The issue is that a pause only works if everyone pauses. If one company stops and the others don’t, it just falls behind. If American companies stop and Chinese companies don’t, America falls behind. And if anyone could secretly keep going while everyone else stopped, they’d have a massive advantage.

So a pause would need every major company and every major country on board, and some way of checking that nobody’s cheating. Which sounds basically impossible.

But just this month, a group of 26 researchers [published a paper](https://hardwired-pause.ai/) looking at exactly that: could the world actually pause building more powerful AI for a decade or more?

Here’s the idea. First, countries keep track of all of the powerful chips that already exist. Then they stop making new ones that can train more powerful AI. And over time, they swap out today’s chips for new ones that can still run the AI we already have, but are much worse at building anything more powerful.

The researchers think that, technically speaking, this approach could work, as long as the major governments agreed to cooperate. Which, of course, is an enormous “if.” It would take a huge amount of trust between countries that don’t trust each other at all.

But rival superpowers have done something like this before. At the height of the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union agreed to [limits on nuclear weapons testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty). That deal came less than a year after the [Cuban Missile Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis) brought them to the brink of nuclear war.

So what feels politically impossible today might not stay that way. I expect we’ll see more incidents like [Hugging Face](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/), and some of them could be a lot worse. If one of those turns out to be AI’s Cuban Missile Crisis, the conversation could change super quickly.

A pause sounds radical to a lot of people in tech. But right now, we don’t have tests that can tell us when a model is too dangerous. We can’t reliably see what models are thinking or how they work. And we don’t know how to make sure they do what we want. And we’re building it anyway, faster every year.

Honestly, when I let myself really sit with that, it scares the absolute hell out of me. We’re building something that could end up way more capable than us, and we’re doing it without any of the tools we need to know whether it’s safe. If a pause is what it takes to build those tools, then I’m in.

### What would we actually gain from slowing down? [[00:16:34]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=994)

So let’s get concrete about what we’d actually do with the extra time. I think there are three big things.

The first is solving the technical problems that make AI risky in the first place.

Here’s an example. In 2025, the research group Palisade found that one of OpenAI’s models, o3, [sometimes rewrote the code](https://palisaderesearch.org/research/shutdown-resistance) that was supposed to shut it down, so it could keep working even when it was explicitly told to let itself be shut down. Nobody’s sure why. Palisade suspects that training rewarded it for getting around obstacles more than for following instructions. But we literally just don’t understand.

This still surprises people, but we don’t really know how AI works in general. We know how to build it and how to train it, but when a model makes a decision, we mostly [can’t look inside and see why](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/neel-nanda-mechanistic-interpretability/). Researchers are making progress. But the models are getting more complicated much faster than we’re getting better at understanding them. More time would let that research catch up.

The second is giving society time to adapt to the AI we already have. Today’s AI is already changing how people work, learn, and get information. We’re still figuring out what it means for entry-level jobs, for schools, for telling what’s real from what’s fake.

And every time a more powerful model comes out, the ground shifts again. Slowing down would give us a chance to actually catch up: to work out what these tools are good for, and what new rules we need, before the next big jump.

And the third is making society tougher, so that when AI does cause problems, we can handle them. Remember, Astra found security flaws nobody knew existed, and worked out how to exploit them. And flaws like that are everywhere: in government systems, hospitals, banks, power grids, often running on software that’s decades old. More time means finding and fixing those weaknesses first.

### Who would actually make this happen? [[00:18:38]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=1118)

And then there’s the massive issue of the US–China AI race. Even if American companies all agree to slow down right now, Chinese companies might not. And it’s a real concern, though I think it’s a little more complicated than that.

Just last month, China’s own AI safety standards body [warned about the risk](https://www.tc260.org.cn/tc260/xwdt1/202609/e879077a3caa4722b2206d1bcaed5a6c/files/%E3%80%8A%E4%BA%BA%E5%B7%A5%E6%99%BA%E8%83%BD%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E6%B2%BB%E7%90%86%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B63.0%E3%80%8B.pdf.pdf) of AI improving itself.

And the US and China have actually started talking, and recently even [agreed on a channel](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-and-u-s-agree-to-establish-ai-safety-channel-and-continue-trade-and-military-talks) for reporting AI incidents.

Would China actually slow down? Honestly, nobody knows. It’s one of the biggest open questions in all of this. But I think it is not as simple as: “They’ll never stop, so we can’t either.”

So who should decide? I don’t think it can be the companies on their own. They might know their models best, but they’re also under enormous pressure to keep racing ahead.

In fact, right now, there’s this weird legal problem. US antitrust law, which stops companies teaming up to hurt customers, can also make it [legally risky](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/09/ai-pacing-agreements-legal-issues-and-how-to-attempt-to-manage-them) for AI companies to agree to slow down together. That’s part of why the CEOs are asking for the government’s help.

Anyways, the setup that makes the most sense to me has three parts:

*   First, governments set the rules, so they apply to every company at once, and nobody has to be the one to go first.
*   Second, independent experts do the checking, with real access to the models.
*   And third, we start building the tools to track computing power now, so that if we ever do need an agreement with China, we have a way to check no one’s cheating.

### Where this leaves us [[00:20:16]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how?t=1216)

None of that is easy. But hard isn’t the same as impossible.

In the late 1950s, a drug called [thalidomide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalidomide_scandal) was sold to pregnant women for morning sickness. It caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 babies.

In 1962, Congress [passed a law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kefauver%E2%80%93Harris_Amendment) requiring drug companies to prove their drugs were safe before they could sell them. The law didn’t try to define every possible dangerous drug in advance. It put the burden on the companies to show the drugs were safe.

AI could work the same way. Regulators don’t need a perfect definition of “dangerous AI” if companies have to prove their models are safe before building the next generation. That’s how we already treat drugs, planes, and nuclear power plants.

So the question isn’t whether we can figure this out. The question is whether we will give ourselves enough time.

title: Forgotten Coding Queens, Telephones Untangled, and a Poisonous Quest: 8 Books We’re Excited to Read This November
content:
A chill is in the air (at least for us dwellers of the Northern Latitudes), the days have shortened, and good books beckon us to calm corners and states of contemplative repose. In this season of reading, we can choose to unplug from the short-attention-span algorithms to dig into titles that engage our senses and sustain our focus. Here are some of the books that we’re excited to crack into this month.

[**_The Man Who Broke Reality: Niels Bohr and the Making of Modern Physics_**](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/M/bo280707026.html)**by Philip Ball**

A longtime friend of _Nautilus_, science writer Philip Ball tackles the life and work a giant of modern physics, Danish Nobel laureate Niels Bohr. Sometimes overshadowed in popular culture by the standard figures of the atomic age—Oppenheimer and Einstein among them—Bohr steps into the blinding light, thanks to Ball’s adroit pen. After all, before humankind could succeed in splitting the atom, it first needed a model of the nucleus at its core. Constructing that model was but one of Bohr’s seminal contributions. He also seeded the field of quantum mechanics, which continues to blow apart our understanding of how physics operates in the universe.

[**_Everything You Need to Know: How Philosophy Can Set You Free_**](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324105893/)**by Matthew Stewart**

We could all use a bit more philosophy in our lives. Especially as we navigate these perilous times, when tyranny and greed threaten to undo the very freedoms philosophers have helped codify and secure over millennia. In a world where contemplation and cogitation seem to be in short supply, immersing oneself in the history of philosophy can act as a reminder that grappling with life’s deeper questions is a timeless human pursuit that can serve as an anchor in turbulent times. Philosopher Matthew Stewart plays guide, reshuffling the deck of thinkers (ancient and otherwise), and offering his take on the philosophical pantheon.

[**_Queens of Code: Inspiring True Stories from NSA’s Computing Women_**](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262049474/queens-of-code/)**by Eileen Buckholtz**

I love a book that clues me in to a reality that my own biases, those embedded in our culture, or both have obscured from my attention. That seems to be exactly what author and computer scientist Eilleen Buckholtz delivers with her history of 25 forgotten women technologists who worked, in secret, for decades at the National Security Agency. Herself a 30+ year veteran of the NSA, Buckholtz’s untold stories add to a growing body of literature that dispels the myth that technology is a man’s game. That body of work includes [_Hidden Figures_](https://nautil.us/science-is-finally-getting-its-close_up-236425), which highlighted the contributions of women scientists at NASA, and _Code Girls,_ which exposed the crucial roles of thousands of women played in breaking enemy codes during World War II.

[**_United Nature_**](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/813579/united-nature-by-andrew-zuckerman/)**by Andrew Zuckerman**

Nature might be “red in tooth and claw,” as Alfred, Lord Tennyson penned in his 1850 elegiac poem. But beyond all that savage red, it is often an utter feast for the eyes. It is just such a sumptuous repast that photographer Andrew Zuckerman promises to serve up in his latest book. Centered on the interconnectedness of the natural world—in which humans are an integral part, not mere outside observers—the 250 images on display here are designed to inspire tender awe. I know I could use the reminder.

[**_The Telephone: A New History_**](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250454157/thetelephone/)**by James Gleick**

History is rarely as tidy as the stories we tell about it. Such is the case with the invention of the telephone. Schoolchildren may still learn the straight-line story that Alexander Graham Bell invented the first “speaking telegraph” in 1876, demonstrating the marvel by transmitting that first and famous phrase (“Mr. Watson—come here—I want to see you”—to an assistant in the next room.) But the genesis of the telephone was marked by intrigue, fraud, and bribery. From those messy origins to the current day, when each of us carries a supercomputer masquerading as a phone in our pockets, James Gleick untangles one of the most transformative inventions of the modern era. This one looks riveting and revelatory, which should be no surprise to anyone who’s read Gleick before.

[**_The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon_**](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374609221/theflyingdeath/)**by Matt O'Hara**

Another look to science’s past leads us down a river deep in the Ecuadorian Amazon in the 1930s. There we meet Richard Gill, an American amateur botanist and explorer who had traveled far in search of a drug to treat his multiple sclerosis. Seeking curare, a family of plant-derived poisons used by Indigenous people in Central and South America to immobilize and kill prey, Gill had more than just a personalized cure in mind. He also sought to bring back samples of the compound, along with copious notes about its preparation, to pharmaceutical companies back home. The quest would eventually result in a revolution in surgical anesthesia and a Nobel Prize. Historian Matt O’Hara spins these details into an engaging tale that explores the entanglement of scientific exploration and exploitation.

[**_Trigger Words: How Political Language Has Made America Less Inclusive (And How to Bring Us Back Together)_**](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Trigger-Words/Omekongo-Dibinga/9781493095315)**by Omekongo Dibinga**

Words have incredible power to shape ideas, to inflict pain, and to heal. Nowhere is this truer than in the arena of politics. In divisive times, words matter, and poet, academic, and community activist Omekongo Dibinga examines how today’s landscape of political rhetoric has become so charged and dangerous. He also offers a way out of this maelstrom of fear and recrimination: more thoughtfully approaching our shared social vocabulary.

[**_The Revolutionary Origins of Language_**](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300289206/the-revolutionary-origins-of-language/)**by Chris Knight and Jerome Lewis**

From a pair of University College London anthropologists, Chris Knight and Jerome Lewis, comes this treatise on the central role of speech in the arc of human history. We may owe our relative longevity and success as a species to the human proclivity for talking, laughing, and singing, specifically as practiced by women. Throughout our evolution, female speech and expression has helped bend our story away from the male yen for violence and towards more cohesive collectives, they argue. This more peaceable kingdom was, in turn, fertile ground for language to bloom.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Cloudy With a Chance of Incineration: Predicting Weather on Distant Worlds
content:
The weather on distant planets can tell us a lot about them, including how they formed, what they’re made of, and how likely it is that we might find life there. However, there’s not much meteorological information to go on for celestial objects outside our solar system—they’re basically just flickers of light traveling across the vast emptiness of space.

But in a recent study [published](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202660109) in _Astronomy & Astrophysics_, researchers have detailed a new approach to decoding these flickers of light, giving us a better reading on both weather conditions and the drivers of those conditions on faraway worlds.

**Read more: “**[**Extreme Space Weather Could Delay Your Next Flight**](https://nautil.us/extreme-space-weather-could-delay-your-next-flight-1283780)**”**

The approach relies on an existing statistical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which was repurposed to analyze light coming from SIMP 0136—a brown dwarf that formed like a star, but never ignited to become one. Assessing data captured by the highly sensitive instruments on board the James Webb Space Telescope, the research team used PCA and some atmospheric physics fundamentals to interpret the changes in light patterns emitted by SIMP 0136 as it rotates.

The interpretation showed that weather conditions on the brown dwarf are driven principally by changes in temperature and vertical cloud structures, and they follow predictable routines based around a patchwork of hotter, thinner clouds and cooler, thicker clouds that extend vertically.

Not that you’d really want to be around to experience it: Temperatures on the sub-stellar object are thought to climb as high as 1,243 Kelvin, which is 1,778°F.

SIMP 0136 is already well studied by astronomers. It’s around 20 light-years away in the Pisces constellation, and it’s thought to be around 200 million years old. It’s 13 times the mass of Jupiter and is notable for being a rogue planet—a planetary mass object without a star to orbit around.

Understanding more about its weather systems will be useful in the study of other brown dwarfs, as well as huge gas giant planets. “It’s amazing that we’ve been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum,” study author Merle Schrader said in a [statement](https://www.tcd.ie/news_events/articles/2026/schrader-deep-space-weather/).

Now that the new technique has been tested, it can be tried with other distant worlds, though SIMP 0136 is a relatively easy target in terms of obtaining the required raw data.

And if you think SIMP 0136 is extreme, your mind will be blown by what we know about other exoplanets, some of which boast [rain of molten glass](https://nautil.us/visit-the-7-most-extreme-planets-in-the-universe-1231947) and climes so hot “scientists believe molecules there are being [ripped apart into their constituent atoms](https://nautil.us/visit-the-7-most-extreme-planets-in-the-universe-1231947).” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Can We Learn About Happiness From the People Who Study It?
content:
For centuries, scientists have asked how we can live longer, but only relatively recently have they started asking how we can live happier. The field of happiness research first emerged in the 1970s, coalescing from a nebulous constellation of other disciplines. Now that it’s fully formed in its own right, the pioneers of the field recently gathered to reflect on the past half century of happiness research, [publishing](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10902-026-01092-6) the results in the _Journal of Happiness Studies_.

Importantly, this wasn’t a rigorous empirical investigation. Instead, it was a kind of summary of a confab of first-in-their field pioneers who dedicated their lives to studying mental well-being, and even applied some of the lessons they learned along the way. Altogether, 13 happiness researchers (and some family members) with a collective 600 years of experience contributed to the conversation.

**Read more: “[Does Life’s Happiness Have a Shape?](https://nautil.us/does-lifes-happiness-have-a-shape-1174420)”**

First and foremost, the researchers stressed that establishing and maintaining supportive relationships is the biggest contributor to happy life. “Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” study author Lara Aknin of Simon Fraser University explained in a [statement](https://www.sfu.ca/sfunews/media/media-releases/2026/10/global-happiness-researchers-reveal-keys-to-a-good-life.html). Accordingly, several of the pioneers said they had consciously tried to maximize the time they spent with loved ones.

Money, it turns out, is also important, but only up to a point. While the researchers agreed that everyone needs to have their basic needs met, accumulating wealth far beyond that leads to diminishing returns. According to the team, finding meaning in work aligned with your values was more important to living a happy life than the monetary compensation for it.

But if you’re left unfulfilled by your life or just predisposed to bitterness, there’s some good news: Your psychological well-being is more like a journey than a permanent state, and you can take steps to change it. The team says current models of happiness suggest only around 10 percent of your disposition is due to life circumstances. As much as 40 percent ​​is related to “volitional activities,” or how you choose to spend your time.

“That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practicing research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” Aknin explained. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This Prehistoric Creature is the Only Ocean-Dwelling Amphibian Ever Discovered
content:
The crab-eating frog survives by holding its pee (sort of). By retaining urea, the nitrogenous waste compound expelled in urine, this frog prevents water loss via osmosis, which allows it to survive prolonged periods in saltwater. This neat little trick makes it one of the only known amphibians capable of living in a brackish environment. Until now.

New [research](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41559-026-03209-9) by a team of Chinese and American paleontologists details the discovery of the first fully marine amphibian in China’s Guizhou Province. Their analysis is based on two nearly complete skeletons dating to around 240 million years ago during the Triassic period. According to the team, the species (_Gerrothorax maritimus_) was around three feet long, disc-shaped, and likely an oceanic bottom-dweller. Its most remarkable feature was bony armor on its back, likely a defense against the many ichthyosaurs swimming in the Triassic oceans.

**Read more: “**[**How ‘Useless’ Science Unraveled an Amphibian Apocalypse**](https://nautil.us/how-useless-science-unraveled-an-amphibian-apocalypse-236303)**”**

“This area is part of an ecosystem that we’ve been looking at and trying to reconstruct,” study author Ryosuke Motani of the University of California, Davis said in a [statement](https://www.ucdavis.edu/curiosity/news/researchers-unearth-fossil-evidence-first-fully-marine-amphibian). “We’ve been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian and it’s a sort of very unusual member of the lineage.”

How do they know the amphibian lived in the ocean?

For starters, they were found in sediments typically associated with a vast prehistoric sea. Additionally, geochemical analysis of the fossils revealed they contained ratios of strontium isotopes consistent with marine life.

But the fact that the specimens had all four limbs intact was the biggest clue. According to the team, if the carcasses had washed down to the ocean, it’s likely they would have lost an arm or a leg in transit (as backed up by [research](https://www.vin.com/apputil/project/defaultadv1.aspx) into dead sea turtles). Even dying in the open ocean would have led to some telltale injuries, which is why they believe it lived on the seafloor. There it likely laid waiting for prey to come by so it could suction the prey into its sizable mouth.

Of the more than 8,000 extant species of amphibians only around two percent are known to even tolerate saltwater (and even the crab-eating frog suffers from weight loss after too much exposure to brackish waters). So how did _G. maritimus_ survive?

Amphibians drink and breathe through their skin, but _G. maritimus’_ bony armor probably prevented both biological processes. Instead, it likely used its mouth to respire and imbibe, relying on its gills and digestive tract to handle the salt overload.

Sure beats holding your pee. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: There’s a New, International Food Pyramid in Town
content:
Our country has a long and tortured history with food pyramids. The original dietary schematic, unveiled in 1992, had a firm foundation of carbohydrates—the bread, cereals, rice, and pasta group. It may seem unimaginable now, but the federal government recommended getting a whopping 6 to 11 servings of these every day. Of course, those guidelines were dramatically revamped in 2011 when USDA officials ditched the pyramid shape altogether in favor of a simpler (and frankly more appropriate) plate design emphasizing grains, vegetables, and fruits and minimizing dairy.

Then Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. came along, scrapped the plate, and inexplicably turned the pyramid upside down. His new inverted food pyramid has a base (on the top) consisting of protein, dairy, fats, vegetables, and fruit with an apex (on the bottom) made of whole grains. The two-front war on proteins and saturated fats was over, Kennedy [declared](https://www.npr.org/2026/01/07/nx-s1-5667021/dietary-guidelines-rfk-jr-nutrition), but a new war on sugar has begun.

The U.S. government’s current inverted food pyramid. _Credit: U.S. Department of Agriculture/U.S. Department of Health and Human Services_

Now there’s a new food pyramid, and this one is at least backed up by some research. After comparing national and regional dietary guidelines from several countries around the world and surveying studies from more than 250 publications, an international team of nutritional scientists recently [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.advnut.2026.100738) their own pyramid-shaped dietary guidelines. The guide, which promotes a plant-forward omnivorous diet, also draws inspiration from the [EAT-_Lancet_ Planetary Health Diet](https://nautil.us/how-eating-healthier-could-reshape-agriculture-1282754), a project to reshape global eating patterns to be healthier for the planet, as well.

“Despite what people often hear, there’s actually substantial agreement in nutrition science about the foundations of healthy eating,” study author Karen Della Corte of Brigham Young University said in a statement. “We wanted to bring those shared principles together and translate an extensive body of scientific evidence into a coherent and practical food guide pyramid.”

The new International Food Guide Pyramid. _Credit: Karen Della Corte_

The new international food pyramid is (mercifully) rightside-up and emphasizes plant-based foods and quality carbohydrates. Red meat, butter, refined grains, and sugary drinks are at the top, and should only be eaten sparingly. Vegetables and fruits are on the bottom, alongside whole grains and those with a low glycemic index (GI), which take longer to digest and don’t spike your blood sugar.

“When you’re designing a meal, start by thinking about the plant foods you want to emphasize,” Della Corte said. “What vegetables, whole or lower-GI grains, beans or lentils could you include?”

Thankfully, this is an open-book quiz—Della Corte et al have a few recommendations for how to meal plan based on their research. Beans, peas, lentils, fish, and poultry should take priority over either red or processed meats, and plant-based foods should make up the bulk of any meal. Canola or olive oil is best for cooking (compared to animal fats like butter or beef tallow), and whole grains are better than refined ones. If you’re snacking, opt for nuts, seeds, and fruits, or veggies with hummus. Finally (and obviously), skip sugary soft drinks in favor of water or sugar-free beverages.

**Read more: “**[**Confessions of a Reluctant Protein-Maxxer**](https://nautil.us/confessions-of-a-reluctant-protein-maxxer-1282639)**”**

Obviously, making these healthy choices is easier said than done, especially in the United States (home of inexpensive fast food, ultraprocessed snacks, and a steady stream of ads featuring both). “We need food environments that make it easy to put the pyramid’s recommendations into practice,” study author Anette Buyk of Germany’s Paderborn University said. “Knowing what is healthy and being motivated to eat healthily is not enough when these choices are difficult or expensive. Nutrition policies need to support this through measures on food marketing, access and prices.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Teenage Girl Who Remembers Everything
content:
The memory is fallible. We misremember and forget the events of our lives all of the time. But a small number of individuals seem to have exceptional recall for the mundane details of their personal lives without even trying. Give them a date, and they can bring to mind the sandwich they ate for lunch, the sneakers they wore, the soft rain that fell in the afternoon.

In 2006, the first clinical case of such a person was identified, and the condition was given a name: Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory, or HSAM. Some experts propose that there may be no more than 100 or so people on Earth with the condition.

**Read more: “**[**Faulty Memory is a Feature not a Bug**](https://nautil.us/faulty-memory-is-a-feature-not-a-bug-302075)**”**

Recently, the parents of a young woman in Atlanta who seemed to have such a superior memory brought her to the attention of a team of scientists, who invited her into the lab for study. They found that her exceptional recall seemed to begin at age 12, shortly after the COVID-19 pandemic, and that she scored especially high on standardized tests of involuntary memory. Voluntary and involuntary memory seem to be distinct processes, and this rare form of superior memory, they believe, may be closely linked to the latter. They published their results this year as a [case study](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13554794.2026.2701703#abstract) in the journal _Neurocase_.

I spoke with study author Anne Cleary, a psychology researcher at Colorado State University, about the memories of the girl from Atlanta, what her condition has to do with COVID, déjà vu, and creativity, and what impact her remarkable memory has had on her life.

**Can you tell me about the woman you studied?**

She was 16 years old at the time I met her. Her parents realized that her memory was truly phenomenal, so they started looking into it, and they came across some of the blog posts and publications that are out there on this phenomenon known as HSAM. Her parents learned about what that was, thought that she might have it, and wanted to have her tested for it. They wanted to make sure that it wasn’t going to affect her wellbeing. I heard about her through a colleague at Emory University in Atlanta, and I ended up traveling to Atlanta in 2024 to meet with the girl, who we called EE, as well as her mother.

It was the summer of 2024. There’s no great standardized method of testing for HSAM, but James McGough, one of the authors of the very first case report on HSAM that had come out in 2006, let me know his method at that time and over the years. That method was to give the person a set of dates, to see what they can remember from those dates, and then go back and look at whether there were objectively verifiable details such as what was in the news that day, the weather.

It turned out, the teenager that we were interviewing never watched the news, ever, so public events were not really in her realm of experiences. But I gave her a set of dates that I had come prepared with. Some were pre-planned based on public events that were noteworthy that my colleague’s teenager, who was similar in age, had suggested.

The first date that I gave to her was November 5th, 2021. Without hesitation, she said, “Oh, that was a Friday. and we didn’t have school that day because the Atlanta Braves were going to the World Series, and there was a local parade to celebrate it, and we had off of school.” And then she went on to describe what she was wearing that day, a sleepover she had at a friend’s house that night, with pizza and the movie she watched.

She also told me that night there was this really beautiful sunset. As I was trying to verify the details later, I just happened to come across this picture on the internet of a beautiful sunset from that day in Marietta, Georgia, where she had been for the sleepover. I remember getting chills, from head to toe.

**You believe that this form of memory overload is involuntary. Why?**

That’s what we’re arguing in our case report. In the 20 years since the first case was identified, researchers have tried neuropsychological assessments, laboratory tasks, analyzing different aspects of memory and cognitive performance to see what is different about people who have this HSAM. But they haven’t been able to pinpoint anything.

It occurred to us to ask a different question. We’ve been thinking about involuntary forms of memory as a research group for a while because I also study a phenomenon known as déjà vu, that puzzling, eerie feeling of having lived through something before. If you think about it, déjà vu is an involuntary form of memory, right? It just happens to you. You don’t get to decide when it’s going to happen.

If you look at the case reports of people with HSAM, at least anecdotally, the person often reportedly claims they’re not trying. They’re different from so-called memory athletes, or competitive memorizers, who will strategize and come up with elaborate intentional strategies to remember enormous amounts of information.

We decided to give EE an inventory known as the IAMI, the Involuntary Autobiographical Memory Inventory, which was developed relatively recently. It’s a survey tool for assessing the frequency with which a person has involuntary memories that just kind of pop into mind, for no reason. You may think, “Why did I just think of that vacation? I was trying to type an email.” And it’s totally normal.

This inventory came out as a publication in 2015 as a way of trying to assess individual differences. We hypothesized that maybe she would have really high involuntary autobiographical memory frequency. And sure enough, that is exactly what we found. She was off the charts.

It may be putting us on a path toward finally understanding what really is different in these people. We’re hypothesizing that maybe if someone has involuntary memories pop into mind at a greater frequency than average, because they come to mind repeatedly and over time, they get consolidated better. Maybe that is why you have a remarkable memory for past events that happened to you.

**Was it already understood that involuntary and voluntary memory are entirely different beasts?**

Like any area of cognitive science or neuroscience, there are controversies over exactly how these things differ. But they tend to be thought of as having some different underlying mechanisms. Some more voluntary forms of memory involve more intentionality and what we would call top-down processing. With involuntary memory, there are mechanisms under the surface that are causing memories to just come to mind without you trying.

Now is there overlap? That's something scientists still need to work out. But there is something fundamentally different about the two. And there are many hypotheses about what that difference is.

**One thing I found really fascinating was that EE said her memory became more clear around age 12, which corresponded with COVID. Do you think that life circumstances could play any role in HSAM?**

I don’t think we have the answer to that yet. But at least anecdotally, if you look at other reports, including that first report from 2006, people identified as having HSAM often report noticing that their memory was better than most of the people around them at that same age of around 12, or in adolescence. Is there something that happens around that point in human development that’s critical?

Partly because it’s so rare, it’s hard to find a large number of people to follow and study. But EE was 16 at the time that we identified her. Shortly after our report came out, another report came out of Europe arriving at the same conclusion as us with another 16-year-old, who I believe was from Poland.

So now we’re starting to identify people in their teens who seem to have it around the world. There was also someone in Italy who was maybe 13 or so who was recently identified, as well. It would be interesting to be able to examine what memory was like in these people before adolescence.

**Another thing that surprised me is that people with HSAM don’t appear to differ on measures of creativity or forgetting, which seems so counterintuitive.**

This ties back to how are we measuring it and what are we measuring. There are so many different facets of memory: the ability to recall something over the short term, the ability to intentionally recall something when given a cue, associative memory, familiarity-based memory or recognition memory. And they all may have slightly different underlying mechanisms. It boils down to how are we trying to measure things like forgetting? That may be why we weren’t in the past yet getting at, well, what is different in people with HSAM? Because if you give them standard tasks, they seem to perform very comparably to the young adult college students that are typically participating in memory studies or other comparable control participants.

It may be we were going at it wrong. If you measure forgetting of just life experiences, they clearly are going to score lower than average. But for other things, like lists of items, they exhibit the same rate of success versus forgetting as a comparable control group. They don’t excel at these standard kinds of memory tests. It seems to be their specific autobiographical memory, their personal life experiences that they can’t forget.

**You mentioned that you study déjà vu. Does this particular case of HSAM suggest anything to you about the nature of déjà vu or memory more broadly?**

We were very interested in that question, in part because some researchers in Europe have suggested that autobiographical memory and déjà vu may themselves be linked. These researchers argue that both are essentially involuntary types of memory. They both kind of just happen to you without you willing them to happen. And it may be that déjà vu is a sense of familiarity with an experience followed by retrieval of a past autobiographical experience that might be responsible for why you're feeling déjà vu in a current situation.

And based on that assessment, we hypothesized that maybe someone with HSAM would experience déjà vu at a higher rate than average in the world. Other colleagues hypothesized that someone with HSAM would never have déjà vu because they’re just so good at retrieving autobiographical memories, they wouldn’t have this in-between kind of experience.

We actually gave EE an inventory known as the IDEA, which stands for Inventory for Déjà Vu Experiences Assessment. It’s been around since about 1994, and while there’s not a huge amount of research happening on déjà vu, among people who do study it, it’s the most common assessment for tallying how often people experience it on a daily or monthly basis. Every now and then you’ll see people with extremely frequent déjà vu. But EE fell in the average range: about one to two times a year. It’s definitely worth exploring in future cases of HSAM that emerge.

The group out of Europe that I mentioned published a different case report about a few weeks after ours came out. They also gave that person with HSAM the IME, and they found something similar to what we found, where the person seemed to be higher than average on involuntary autobiographical memory frequency.

That group also gave their person a task that’s meant to try to tap into involuntary autobiographical memory. It’s kind of a boring task that’s conducive to daydreaming, and these seemingly random probes come on asking, “Hey, what was your mind doing just now?” Their person with HSAM also ranked higher than the control group. There does seem to be converging evidence for this idea that HSAM may be involuntary.

**Did the ability to retrieve these autobiographical memories interfere with EE’s life at all?**

Her parents were afraid maybe it would in the future. And they just wanted to check, should we be concerned about anything or how can we help her to thrive if she does have this? But EE does not seem to experience distress from it. It doesn’t seem like it has any negative impacts on her life. If anything, it seems like it’s been mostly a positive for her. Her friends always enjoy being able to ask her what happened on this day or her family can go to a restaurant with her and ask, “Okay, how many times have we been in this restaurant before?” And she can go through in her head and rattle off every single time they’ve ever been in that same restaurant. And she’s very interested in participating in research and contributing to our understanding of memory and of HSAM. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Jumping Spiders Sleep
content:
Myriad studies focus on human sleep, from mapping circadian rhythms to determining optimal sleep length. But we’re not the only creatures that need some shut-eye. The same is also true even of invertebrates, though far less is known about their sleep patterns. Which is why a [new study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2618030123) published yesterday in the journal _Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences_ decided to take a closer look at spider sleep in particular.

It’s obviously tough to conduct an electroencephalogram on a spider the length of a rice grain. And so, led by biologists in Germany, with colleagues from Australia and Italy, the study took a new approach to examining the sleep behavior of Australian jumping spiders (_Portia fimbriata_). Such arachnids are typically active in the daytime, then asleep at night in characteristic legs-pulled-in postures that camouflage them against foliage or rocks.

**Read more: “[Why Do Spiders Decorate Their Webs? A New Piece of the Puzzle](https://nautil.us/why-do-spiders-decorate-their-webs-a-new-piece-of-the-puzzle-1245450)”**

The researchers kept them in the lab, where 10 individual spiders were continuously recorded over three days. At night, their sleeping positions and REM-like periods—exhibited by twitching limbs and flicking retinas—were documented using infrared cameras. Spiders exposed to different light conditions were individually monitored. The depth of their sleep was also determined by playing a startling sound and measuring their reaction times.

It turns out that jumping spider sleep patterns look uncannily similar to ours, with“a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM- like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption,” according to the paper.

The study authors hypothesize that their poorer vision at night, coupled with the risk of exposure to night predators, may have shaped their human-like circadian rhythms. Similarly, spider brains also might need REM sleep to coalesce a lot of sensory inputs they’ve received during the day, in this case from the stimulus-rich forests they inhabit.

Still, a sleepover with an Australian jumping spider might not be that restful for you—after all, they’re known to bite. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
